title: Part 3, Chapter 4
paragraphs: At that moment the door opened softly and a young girl walked into the room, looking timidly around. Everyone turned toward her with surprise and curiosity. At first Raskolnikov didn't recognize her. It was Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladov. He had seen her for the first time yesterday, but under such circumstances, in such surroundings and wearing such clothes, that his memory held a very different picture. Now she was a modestly and poorly dressed young girl, very young indeed, almost a child, with a quiet and refined manner and a candid but somewhat frightened-looking face. She wore a very plain house dress and a shabby, old-fashioned hat, but still carried a parasol. Finding the room unexpectedly full of people, she was not so much embarrassed as completely overwhelmed with shyness, like a small child. She was even about to back away. "Oh, it's you!" said Raskolnikov, extremely astonished, and he too was confused. He immediately recalled that his mother and sister knew from Luzhin's letter about "some young woman of notorious behaviour." He had just been protesting against Luzhin's slander and declaring that he had seen the girl for the first time last night, and now here she was. He also remembered that he hadn't protested against the words "of notorious behaviour." All this flashed vaguely and fleetingly through his mind, but looking at her more intently, he saw that this humiliated creature was so humiliated that he suddenly felt sorry for her. When she moved to retreat in terror, it sent a pang through his heart.
"I didn't expect you," he said hurriedly, with a look that made her stop. "Please sit down. You've come from Katerina Ivanovna, no doubt. Not there, please. Sit here."

When Sonia entered, Razumihin, who had been sitting on one of Raskolnikov's three chairs near the door, stood up to let her pass. Raskolnikov first motioned her toward the sofa where Zossimov had been sitting, but then, feeling that the sofa—which served as his bed—was too intimate a place, he hastily directed her to Razumihin's chair.
"You sit here," he said to Razumihin, putting him on the sofa.

Sonia sat down, nearly shaking with nerves, and looked timidly at the two ladies. It was clearly almost inconceivable to her that she could sit beside them. The thought so frightened her that she quickly stood up again and, in utter confusion, addressed Raskolnikov.

"I—I've come for just a minute. Forgive me for disturbing you," she began haltingly. "I come from Katerina Ivanovna, and she had no one else to send. She told me to ask you to be at the service tomorrow morning at Mitrofanievsky, and then to come to us—to her—to do her the honour. She told me to ask you." Sonia stammered and fell silent.

"I'll certainly try, most certainly," Raskolnikov answered. He too had stood up, and he too faltered and couldn't finish his sentence. "Please sit down," he said suddenly. "I want to talk to you. You may be in a hurry, but please spare me two minutes." And he pulled up a chair for her.
Sonia sat down again, and again she cast a timid, frightened glance at the two ladies before dropping her eyes. Raskolnikov's pale face flushed, a shudder ran through him, and his eyes blazed.

"Mother," he said firmly and insistently, "this is Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladov, the daughter of that unfortunate Mr. Marmeladov who was run over before my eyes yesterday, and whom I was just telling you about."

Pulcheria Alexandrovna glanced at Sonia and slightly narrowed her eyes. Despite her unease before Rodya's urgent and challenging look, she couldn't deny herself that small satisfaction. Dounia gazed gravely and intently at the poor girl's face, studying her with bewilderment. Sonia, hearing herself introduced, tried to raise her eyes again but was more embarrassed than ever.
"I wanted to ask you," Raskolnikov said hastily, "how things went yesterday. You weren't troubled by the police, for instance?"
"No, that was fine. The cause of death was too obvious. They didn't bother us. Only the other tenants are angry."
"Why?"
"About the body remaining so long. You see, it's hot now. So today they'll carry it to the cemetery chapel until tomorrow. At first Katerina Ivanovna was unwilling, but now she sees it's necessary."
"Today, then?"
"She asks you to do us the honour of attending the church service tomorrow, and then the funeral lunch."
"She's giving a funeral lunch?"
"Yes, a small one. She told me to thank you very much for helping us yesterday. Without you, we would have had nothing for the funeral."
Suddenly her lips and chin began trembling, but she controlled herself with an effort, looking down again.

During the conversation, Raskolnikov studied her carefully. She had a thin, very thin, pale little face, rather irregular and angular, with a sharp little nose and chin. She couldn't have been called pretty, but her blue eyes were so clear, and when they lit up, there was such kindness and simplicity in her expression that you couldn't help being drawn to her. Her face—and her whole figure—had another distinctive quality. Despite her eighteen years, she looked almost like a little girl, almost a child. And in some of her gestures, this childishness seemed almost comical.
"But has Katerina Ivanovna been able to manage on such small means? Does she really plan to have a funeral lunch?" Raskolnikov asked, deliberately keeping the conversation going.

"The coffin will be plain, of course, and everything simple, so it won't cost much. Katerina Ivanovna and I have figured it all out, and there'll be enough left over. She was very anxious that it be done properly. You know how she is."
"I understand, of course. Why are you looking at my room like that? My mother just said it's like a tomb."

"You gave us everything yesterday," Sonia said suddenly in reply, in a loud, rapid whisper, and she looked down again in confusion. Her lips and chin trembled once more. She had been struck at once by Raskolnikov's impoverished surroundings, and the words broke out of her spontaneously. A silence followed. Dounia's eyes softened, and even Pulcheria Alexandrovna looked kindly at Sonia.

"Rodya," she said, getting up, "we'll have dinner together, of course. Come, Dounia. And you, Rodya, should go for a little walk and then rest and lie down before you come to see us. I'm afraid we've worn you out."
"Yes, yes, I'll come," he answered, getting up fussily. "But I have something to attend to."
"But surely you'll have dinner together?" Razumihin cried, looking at Raskolnikov in surprise. "What do you mean?"
"Yes, yes, I'm coming, of course! And you stay a moment. You don't need him right now, do you, mother? Or perhaps I'm keeping him from you?"
"Oh, no, not at all. And will you, Dmitri Prokofitch, do us the favor of dining with us?"
"Please do," added Dounia.
Razumihin bowed, positively beaming. For a moment they were all strangely embarrassed.
"Goodbye, Rodya—that is, until later. I don't like saying goodbye. Goodbye, Nastasya. Oh, I've said goodbye again."
Pulcheria Alexandrovna meant to greet Sonia too, but somehow it didn't come off, and she hurried out of the room in a flutter.

But Avdotya Romanovna seemed to wait her turn, and following her mother, gave Sonia an attentive, courteous bow. Sonia, confused, returned a hurried, frightened curtsy. There was a look of painful discomfort on her face, as though Avdotya Romanovna's courtesy and attention were oppressive and distressing to her.
"Dounia, goodbye!" Raskolnikov called from the hallway. "Give me your hand."
"But I already did. Have you forgotten?" said Dounia, turning to him warmly but awkwardly.
"Never mind, give it to me again." And he squeezed her fingers warmly.
Dounia smiled, blushed, pulled her hand away, and went off quite happy.
"Well, that's wonderful," he said to Sonia, going back in and looking at her brightly. "God give peace to the dead—the living must go on living. Isn't that right?"
Sonia was surprised by the sudden brightness in his face. He looked at her for several moments in silence. The entire story of her dead father floated before his memory in those moments.

"Heavens, Dounia," Pulcheria Alexandrovna began as soon as they were in the street, "I actually feel relieved at leaving—more at ease. How little I imagined yesterday on the train that I could ever be glad of that!"
"I'm telling you again, mother, he's still very ill. Don't you see? Maybe worrying about us upset him. We must be patient. Much can be forgiven."

"Well, you weren't very patient yourself!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna shot back, hotly and jealously. "You know, Dounia, looking at you two—you're his very portrait, not so much in looks as in character. You're both melancholy, both moody and hot-tempered, both proud and both generous. Surely he can't be selfish, Dounia? When I think of what's coming this evening, my heart sinks!"
"Don't worry, mother. What must be, will be."
"Dounia, just think what a position we're in! What if Pyotr Petrovitch breaks it off?" poor Pulcheria Alexandrovna blurted out incautiously.
"He won't be worth much if he does," Dounia answered sharply and contemptuously.

"We did well to leave," Pulcheria Alexandrovna hurried on. "He was in a hurry about some business. If he goes out for some fresh air—it's so terribly stuffy in his room. But where can you get fresh air here? Even the streets feel like closed rooms. Good heavens, what a city! Watch out—this way—they'll crush you! They're carrying something. Why, it's a piano! How they push! I'm very much afraid of that young woman, too."
"What young woman, mother?"
"Why, that Sofya Semyonovna who was there just now."
"Why?"
"I have a presentiment, Dounia. Believe it or not, the moment she walked in, that very instant, I felt she was the main cause of the trouble."
"Nothing of the sort!" Dounia cried in exasperation. "What nonsense, with your presentiments, mother! He only met her the evening before, and he didn't even recognize her when she came in."

"Well, you'll see! She worries me. But you'll see, you'll see! I was so frightened. She was staring at me with those eyes. I could barely sit still when he started introducing her—remember? It seems so strange, but Pyotr Petrovitch writes about her that way, and yet he introduces her to us—to you! So he must think very highly of her."
"People will write anything. We were talked about and written about too. Have you forgotten? I'm sure she's a good girl and that it's all nonsense."
"God grant it!"
"And Pyotr Petrovitch is a contemptible slanderer," Dounia snapped.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was crushed. The conversation died.
"I'll tell you what I need from you," said Raskolnikov, drawing Razumihin to the window.
"Then I'll tell Katerina Ivanovna you're coming," Sonia said hurriedly, preparing to leave.

"One moment, Sofya Semyonovna. We have no secrets. You're not in the way. I want another word or two with you. Listen," he turned suddenly to Razumihin, "you know that—what's his name—Porfiry Petrovitch?"
"Of course! He's a relative. Why?" Razumihin added with interest.
"Isn't he handling that case, you know, the murder? You were talking about it yesterday."
"Yes. What about it?" Razumihin's eyes widened.

"He was asking about people who'd pawned things, and I have some pledges there too—trifles—a ring my sister gave me as a keepsake when I left home, and my father's silver watch. They're only worth five or six roubles altogether, but I value them. What should I do now? I don't want to lose them, especially the watch. I was terrified just now that mother might ask to see it, when we were talking about Dounia's watch. It's the only thing we have left of father's. She'd be sick if it were lost. You know how women are. So tell me what to do. I know I should report to the police station, but wouldn't it be better to go straight to Porfiry? What do you think? I'd like to get it settled quickly. You'll see—mother will ask about it before dinner."

"Definitely not the police station. Definitely Porfiry," Razumihin practically shouted, extraordinarily excited. "I'm so glad! Let's go right now. It's just a couple of steps. We'll be sure to find him."
"All right, let's go."

"He'll be absolutely delighted to meet you. I've told him about you many times. I was talking about you just yesterday. Let's go. So you knew the old woman? That's how it all fits together! Oh, yes, Sofya Ivanovna—"
"Sofya Semyonovna," Raskolnikov corrected. "Sofya Semyonovna, this is my friend Razumihin, and he's a good man."
"If you have to go now," Sonia began, not looking at Razumihin at all and even more embarrassed.
"Let's go," Raskolnikov decided. "I'll come to see you today, Sofya Semyonovna. Just tell me where you live."
He wasn't exactly uneasy, but he seemed hurried and avoided her eyes. Sonia gave her address and blushed as she did so. They all went out together.
"Don't you lock up?" Razumihin asked, following him down the stairs.
"Never," Raskolnikov answered. "I've been meaning to buy a lock for two years. People who don't need locks are fortunate," he said, laughing to Sonia. They stopped in the gateway.

"Do you go to the right, Sofya Semyonovna? By the way, how did you find me?" he added, as though he wanted to say something quite different. He wanted to look into her soft, clear eyes, but couldn't manage it.
"Why, you gave your address to Polenka yesterday."
"Polenka? Oh yes, Polenka—the little girl. She's your sister? Did I give her the address?"
"You'd forgotten?"
"No, I remember."

"I'd heard my father speak of you, only I didn't know your name, and he didn't know it either. And today, when I came, I asked, 'Where does Mr. Raskolnikov live?' I didn't know you only rented a room too. Goodbye—I'll tell Katerina Ivanovna."

She was extremely glad to escape at last. She hurried off, looking down, rushing to get out of sight, to reach the turning on the right twenty steps away and at last be alone—then to walk quickly, looking at no one, noticing nothing, thinking, remembering, turning over every word, every detail. Never, never had she felt anything like this. A whole new world was dimly, unconsciously opening before her. She suddenly remembered that Raskolnikov intended to come to her that very day, perhaps right away!
"Only not today, please, not today!" she kept murmuring with a sinking heart, like a frightened child begging. "Mercy! To me, to that room—he'll see—oh God!"

She was incapable at that moment of noticing an unknown gentleman who was watching her and following at her heels. He had trailed her from the gateway. When Razumihin, Raskolnikov, and she had stood saying goodbye on the pavement, this gentleman, who happened to be passing, had caught Sonia's words: "I asked where Mr. Raskolnikov lived." He cast a quick but attentive glance at all three, particularly at Raskolnikov, to whom Sonia was speaking, then noted the house. All of this was done in an instant, and trying not to betray his interest, he walked on more slowly, as if waiting for something. He was waiting for Sonia. He could see they were parting and that she was heading home.
"Home? Where? I've seen that face somewhere," he thought. "I must find out."

At the corner he crossed the street, looked back, and saw Sonia coming the same way, noticing nothing. She turned the corner. He followed on the opposite side. After about fifty paces he crossed back, caught up with her, and stayed two or three yards behind.

He was a man of about fifty, rather tall and solidly built, with broad, high shoulders that made him look as though he stooped slightly. He wore fine, fashionable clothes and looked like a gentleman of position. He carried a handsome cane, which he tapped on the pavement at each step; his gloves were spotless. He had a broad, rather pleasant face with high cheekbones and fresh color not often seen in Petersburg. His flaxen hair was still thick, with only a touch of gray here and there, and his full, square beard was even lighter than his hair. His eyes were blue, with a cold and thoughtful look; his lips were red. He was remarkably well-preserved and looked much younger than his years.

When Sonia reached the canal embankment, they were the only two people on the pavement. He noticed her dreaminess and distraction. When she reached the house where she lived and turned in at the gate, he followed, looking somewhat surprised. In the courtyard she turned toward the right-hand corner. "Well!" the unknown gentleman muttered, and climbed the stairs behind her. Only then did Sonia notice him. She reached the third floor, turned down the corridor, and rang at No. 9. On the door was inscribed in chalk: "Kapernaumov, Tailor." "Well!" the stranger repeated, wondering at the strange coincidence, and rang next door at No. 8. The two doors were only two or three yards apart.
"You live at Kapernaumov's," he said, looking at Sonia and laughing. "He altered a waistcoat for me yesterday. I'm staying right here, at Madame Resslich's. How odd!" Sonia looked at him attentively.
"We're neighbours," he went on cheerfully. "I only arrived in town the day before yesterday. Well, goodbye for now."
Sonia said nothing. The door opened and she slipped inside. She felt somehow ashamed and uneasy, though she couldn't have said why.
On the way to Porfiry's, Razumihin was obviously excited.
"That's wonderful, brother," he repeated several times, "and I'm glad! I'm glad!"
"What are you so glad about?" Raskolnikov thought to himself.
"I didn't know you'd pawned things with the old woman too. Was it long ago? I mean, how long since you were there?"
"What a simple-hearted fool he is!"

"When was it?" Raskolnikov stopped to think. "Two or three days before her death, it must have been. But I'm not going to redeem the things now," he added with a sort of hurried, conspicuous concern about the items. "I've got no more than a silver rouble left after last night's damned delirium!"
He stressed the word "delirium" deliberately.

"Yes, yes," Razumihin hastened to agree—though it wasn't clear with what. "So that's why you were so affected. Partly, you know, in your delirium you kept mentioning rings and chains! Yes, yes, that makes sense. It's all clear now."

"Listen to that! How that idea must have spread among them. This man would go to the stake for me, and he's delighted that it's been 'cleared up' why I mentioned rings in my delirium! What a hold the idea must have on all of them!"
"Will we find him in?" he asked suddenly.

"Oh yes," Razumihin answered quickly. "He's a nice fellow, you'll see, brother. A bit clumsy—I mean, he's a man of polished manners, but clumsy in a different sense. He's intelligent, very much so, but he has his own way of thinking. He's skeptical, cynical, likes to put people on. Or rather, to make fun of them. He uses the old, methodical approach. But he understands his work thoroughly. Last year he solved a murder case where the police had almost no leads. He's very, very eager to meet you!"
"On what grounds?"

"Oh, it's not exactly—you see, since you've been ill, I happened to mention you several times. So when he heard about you, about your being a law student unable to finish your studies, he said, 'What a pity!' And so I figured, from everything together—not just that. Yesterday, Zametov—you know, Rodya, I said some nonsense on our way home yesterday when I was drunk. I'm worried, brother, that you might exaggerate it—"
"What? That they think I'm a madman? Maybe they're right," he said with a strained smile.
"Yes, yes—that is, no, not at all! But everything I said—and there was other stuff too—it was all drunken nonsense."
"Why are you apologizing? I'm so sick of all this!" Raskolnikov exclaimed with exaggerated irritation, though it was partly an act.
"I know, I know, I understand. Believe me, I understand. It's embarrassing to even talk about."
"Then don't."
Both fell silent. Razumihin was more than ecstatic, and Raskolnikov sensed it with disgust. He was also alarmed by what Razumihin had just said about Porfiry.

"I'll have to put on a performance with him too," he thought, his heart pounding as he turned white, "and make it look natural. But the most natural thing would be to do nothing at all. Carefully do nothing! No, 'carefully' wouldn't be natural either. Well, we'll see how it goes. We'll see soon enough. Is it a good thing I'm going or not? The moth flies to the flame. My heart is pounding—that's what's bad!"
"In this grey building," said Razumihin.

"The most important thing: does Porfiry know I was at the old woman's flat yesterday and asked about the blood? I must find that out instantly, as soon as I walk in—read it from his face. Otherwise I'll find out even if it ruins me."
"Listen, brother," he said suddenly to Razumihin with a sly smile, "I've been noticing all day that you seem strangely excited. Am I right?"
"Excited? Not at all," said Razumihin, stung.

"Yes, brother, I assure you it's noticeable. You sat on your chair in a way you never do—right on the edge, squirming the whole time. You kept jumping up for no reason. One minute you were angry, the next your face turned sweet as candy. You even blushed. Especially when you were invited to dinner—you blushed terribly."
"Nothing of the sort! Nonsense! What are you talking about?"
"Why are you squirming like a schoolboy? Good lord, he's blushing again!"
"What a pig you are!"
"But why are you so embarrassed about it? Romeo! Just wait—I'll tell everyone about you today. Ha-ha-ha! That'll give mother a laugh, and someone else too."
"Listen, listen, this is serious! What next, you devil!" Razumihin was utterly beside himself, going cold with horror. "What will you tell them? Come on, brother—what a pig you are!"

"You're like a summer rose! And if you only knew how well it suits you—a Romeo over six feet tall! And how you've washed today—you even cleaned your nails, I do believe. That's unheard of! And is that pomade in your hair? Bend down."
"Pig!"

Raskolnikov laughed as though he couldn't hold it in. And laughing like that, they entered Porfiry Petrovitch's apartment. This was exactly what Raskolnikov wanted: from inside they could be heard laughing as they came in, still guffawing in the hallway.
"Not a word in here, or I'll brain you!" Razumihin whispered furiously, seizing Raskolnikov by the shoulder.
